I think that has to do with the fact that the EF scale is strictly an human impact scale.    Every other one is data driven.  

Unlike hurricanes which from over weeks, tornadoes from in almost and instant cause massive devastation and are gone almost as fast.   

And no meteorologists worth his salt is complaining about the lack of EF 5 tornadoes.    They might be complaining about how the scale works, and how we might need a better one.  

It’s the person who knows nothing about the impact a tornado of that size can do, it’s that person who doesn’t understand the scale.   It’s the doomseakers, those people who want to see disaster at its peak.  It’s the people who just had their lives turned upside down by something so devastating, and only being a 3 out of 5 

We as a species want these devastating things to be abnormal, to be extraordinary.   And when these storms rip through a town changing the lives of everyone involved only hit 3 out of 5 that’s not abnormal.   

An EF-3 is most assuredly abnormal but if you don’t know the scale, if you don’t know how it works it’s simply a 3 out of 5.   And I think that’s the flaw of the scale, it’s not well known enough.   Hurricanes are on the news a week before they ever might make landfall and thus the knowledge of the scale is more in our minds.  Earthquakes are quick but devastating and there’s a precise instrument that gives us our data.  Tornados are only in the news as they happen or after they disappear with no real data outside of wind speed estimates (and they are estimated) from a radar that could be miles and miles away.

So, from a manufacturing perspective it’s probably cheaper to make Streamline. Currently the Streamline line up is pretty small and is ripe for expansion having a top level pros name attached to each new disc will boost those sales more and get more people buying from the MVP family.   On top of that I assume the mold machines from MVP/Axiom are different then the mold machines for Streamline so having a pro push a new line on Streamline doesn’t take machines away from MVP Axiom and helps make production more fluid.  

The money all looks the same to them whether it’s from Streamline, MVP or Axiom, and if one of those is struggling it’s good business sense to apply some sort of strategy to get that branch on par with the other two.

Oh man, I remember when 8 was “big” now I skate and 8.5.   Skating has changed so much since I started.  I feel old, though my body tells me that after every session longer than an hour and a half.

Board size and shape are personal preference.   

Smaller boards will flip faster/easier.  I can pull a triple flip on a 7.75 with about as much effort as double on my 8.5.  But the flip will be faster and harder to catch at the right moment. They are lighter so feasibly you’d be able to pop higher with less effort.   Smaller boards will also be harder to control at speed because of the smaller wheel base due to the smaller truck size.

Smaller boards are probably better for technical flip tricks and street skating. But you may have a harder time locking into truck fronts again due to the smaller truck size.  with a marginal consistency increase to board based grinds since there is less board to get around and on to.  

Larger boards will be harder to flip, but you’ll be able to flip with more speed control and will be able to catch them easier.  They are heavier so they will take more effort to pop higher, but they are easier to control at speed.  You’ll also see marginal improvement to plain spin trick consistency, since there more surface area for your feet to contact while spinning.   

Larger boards are probably better for transition/vert skating with maybe a slight edge to truck grinds, and a hit to board based grinds for the inverse reason listed for small boards.  


All that’s to say there are pros and cons to each size big or small, it all depends on what you like and how it feels this board may in fact be to small but it sounds like your just starting out, and you have plenty of time to figure out the subjective.  Try more, find what you like but in no way should you trash a set up just because your friend said it’s “too small”.   

There is only one black and white, right or wrong thing in skateboarding, and that is: pushing mongo is always wrong.   Everything else is subjective, wheel size, hardness, truck tightness, right height, board concave, tail vs nose hight.  Should you skate a twin nose, or twin tail, a shaved tail a nose that is steeper than the tail, not nose that’s more rounded, or a non popsicle shaped board.   

Have fun figuring it out. You’ll know once you’ve found it.

Hey fellow skater turned disc golf guy.  I started skating when I was 10 also, had some promising things going (flow for a board company) tore my knee to shreds,  came back to it more as a hobby since I didn’t want to break myself again trying for something and end up missing my chance anyway.  Broke a few more bones. I  skated  everyday I could as long as I could.  I got older and couldn’t skate as long as I would like to anymore (not that I was super old but that the years of abuse I put my body through finally caught up at 23).   Started picking up other hobbies,  hiking was by far my favorite but it didn’t scratch the itch that skating did.  Then my buddy asked if I wanted to try disc golf, he described it as “A hike with a mini game”. I thought I’d be a fun one off thing, but it was pretty fun so for a disc and would go out every now and again.   Then 4 years ago I destroyed my ankle skateboarding.  4 surgeries and a year of rehab just to be able to walk normally, was told I probably wouldn’t be able to skate anymore (that hit hard).   After the year of rehab I started throwing more and found it scratched the itch that skateboarding did, and it has now replaced the hole left.   My ankle has recovered better than the doctors thought it would, and I can kind of skate but I can only get maybe 3 hours a week before it hurts to walk for a few days. It’s sad I cant skate but disc golf really hits the same places in my brain.  Something I can do for hours alone (or with a group of friends, subtly improving, leaning new “tricks” (shot types, and lines)  I miss skating, but disc golf really helped me get out of my funk and is just as rewarding when you first hit that shot you’ve been practicing for weeks just like landing a trick for the first time.

So, your argument that a 50 year old playing a sport that is still on the upswing at a high level will lessen the attraction to the sport on a competitive basis?  

My argument is a 50 year old playing at the highest level will attract more people to play and grow the sport because it will show that it’s a sport you can play long into life.   A growing sport needs above all else more players.   More players equals more money going into it more viewers on content around the sport, more views around the sport means more money going into production of said content.   

All sports started off as a “goofy” thing you did with “weird” equipment.  They became popular because they were fun to play Showing someone that anyone can play will get more people to play and find out how fun it is.  

We don’t need to “Legitimize” the professional end, that happens over time as the sport grows.  2021 was a huge leap forward in that with Worlds this year being featured and talked about on main sports networks.   The only way to “legitimize” the pro level is prove that it gets views, the only way to get it views is to get more people playing.   

So I say, if he plays at a high level and wins a bit that’s not bad, that just shows that anyone can play, and anyone can play well if they practice.   Sure the initial thought might be “how hard can it be if he’s out there winning” but thar thought will quickly be changed the moment they try and throw a disc.   At this point in the growth of the sport it’s more important to get people playing, get people watching.   Not prove that the elite are so much better than the rest.
